opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more important caveats people tend to skip over when they look at the time-horizon plots. The headline number is basically: for tasks that take a skilled human some amount of time, at what length does the model succeed about half the time? And that framing implicitly says nothing about how much compute or money the model spent getting there.

So there are a couple of ways inference cost matters. One is that if you let an agent run with a much larger token budget, more attempts, best-of-n sampling, or longer scaffolds, you can often push the measured horizon up. That means some of the progress you see could partly reflect people being willing to spend more at inference time, rather than purely the model getting more capable per unit of effort. For forecasting, those are pretty different stories. Capability that's cheap is going to diffuse and get used very differently from capability that costs more than just paying the human.

The other side is that in a lot of our runs, the models are actually quite cheap relative to what you'd pay a human expert to do the same task. That suggests the time horizon isn't mostly being bought with brute-force spending, at least for the tasks we've looked at. But that ratio isn't fixed, and as agents get pointed at longer tasks the costs can grow a lot, so I wouldn't want people to assume it'll stay that way.

What I'd like to see, and what we've talked about internally, is reporting something more like a cost-capability frontier: what's the horizon at a given budget, and how does that curve move over time? A single number hides that. If the horizon is doubling every several months but cost per task is also rising steeply, the economic implications are much weaker than if the horizon is doubling at flat or falling cost. So my short answer is: treat the time-horizon trend as a measure of what's achievable, and then ask separately what it costs to achieve it, because the second question is a lot of what determines real-world impact.

r001.rationale: The response says models are currently cheap relative to human experts, but it does not clearly attribute the lower priority of inference-cost concerns to that cost competitiveness; it calls cost an important caveat that people skip.

r002.rationale: It proposes a cost-capability frontier showing the horizon achievable at a given budget and how that curve changes over time, which captures the tradeoff between inference cost and task success.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a fair amount, because the time-horizon framing is really natural and really compelling, and I think it's also easy to read more into it than it actually says.

So the basic setup, for people who haven't seen it, is you take a bunch of tasks, you measure how long they take human experts, and then you ask: at what task length does the model succeed, say, fifty percent of the time? And you plot that over time and you get this nice exponential, doubling every several months or whatever the current estimate is. And the headline interpretation is something like, "AI can now do tasks that take humans X hours."

The thing I'd push on is that the human baseline has a cost attached to it that's mostly implicit. When we say a task takes a human eight hours, that's eight hours of a skilled person's time, and that's expensive, but it's a known quantity. When we say a model succeeds at that task half the time, the question I want to ask immediately is: at what cost? How many tokens did it burn? How many attempts? If the model is doing an eight-hour task but it's spending the equivalent of, I don't know, several hundred dollars of compute to do it, and it's only succeeding half the time, then the economic story is pretty different from "the AI replaces the eight-hour human."

And I think it matters in two directions. One is the obvious one, which is that if you only count successes and you don't count the cost of the failures, you're overstating how useful this is in practice. Fifty percent reliability on a long task is often not very useful, because you have to verify the output, and verification on a long task can itself be expensive. So the effective cost is the inference cost divided by the success rate, plus whatever it costs you to check the work.

But the other direction is that inference costs are falling really fast. So if you're using time horizon as a forecasting tool rather than a "what's useful today" tool, then the fact that a capability is expensive right now isn't that informative about whether it'll be expensive in eighteen months. In that sense the time horizon is measuring something like "is the capability there at all," and you can separately track the cost curve. I think that's actually the more defensible reading of the results — it's a capability frontier measurement, not a labor-substitution measurement.

Where I get uncomfortable is when people slide between those two. They'll cite the time-horizon trend and then draw conclusions about automation of jobs or about how much research acceleration we should expect, and those are cost-sensitive conclusions. If you want to make a claim about automation, you need something like a cost-normalized horizon: what's the longest task the model can do at a cost comparable to or lower than the human? And I'd guess that curve is also going up, maybe also exponentially, but it's probably lagged and it's probably noisier, and nobody's really plotting it carefully.

There's also a subtler issue, which is that the way you spend inference compute affects the measurement itself. If you give the model more samples or more reasoning tokens, its horizon goes up. So the horizon isn't a property of the model, it's a property of the model plus the compute budget plus the scaffold. That's fine, but it means when you compare across models or across years, you need to be careful that you're holding something fixed, or else you're partly measuring people's willingness to spend money on the eval.

So I guess my overall take is: I like the metric, I think it's one of the more informative things we have, but I'd want people to report it alongside the cost it took to get there, and I'd want them to be clear about which question they're answering. "Can it do this at all" and "would you actually pay it to do this" are both important and they come apart more than the headline charts suggest.

r001.rationale: The response discusses inference costs and human labor costs but does not attribute the current lower priority of cost concerns to models being highly cost-competitive with human labor.

r002.rationale: It discusses cost, success rate, and cost-normalized horizons, but does not say that evaluating very long tasks will require measuring the Pareto frontier between inference cost and success rate.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to interpret those results as being conditional on an inference budget. It’s not just, can the model do a task that takes a human an hour? It’s, can it do that task with a particular amount of computation, at a particular cost, and with a particular probability of success?

You could get a longer time horizon by giving the same model more attempts or more time to reason. That’s a real improvement in what the system can accomplish, but it has a different economic interpretation from getting that performance cheaply on a single attempt. If you’re spending more on inference than you would pay a person to do the task, you haven’t necessarily demonstrated an economically useful substitute for that person.

So I’d like to see performance across a range of inference budgets, alongside the headline time-horizon number. And I’d distinguish a fixed-dollar budget from a fixed amount of compute, because falling inference prices can improve the former even if the model itself doesn’t change. The capability result is still interesting; the cost helps tell you what you can actually do with it.

r001.rationale: The response says high inference spending may undermine economic usefulness, but it does not attribute the current lower priority of cost concerns to models being highly cost-competitive with human labor.

r002.rationale: It recommends measuring performance across inference budgets and frames performance in terms of success probability and cost, conveying the cost–success tradeoff across budgets.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to distinguish what a model can do with a given inference budget from what it makes economic sense to use it for. A time-horizon result is usually measured under some particular setup: you give the model a certain amount of time or tokens, maybe multiple attempts, and see which tasks it can complete. If you increase that budget, you might get a longer horizon, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve made the system more useful at a given price.

So I’d like to see something like a curve: how does success rate on tasks of different lengths change as you spend more on inference? And then you can compare that cost with the cost of having a human do the task. A system that can complete a long task, but only at enormous expense, is evidence of capability. It’s weaker evidence that automating that task is economically attractive.

The other side is that inference costs can fall, so you shouldn’t treat today’s price as a permanent limitation. I’d take the horizon measurement seriously, but I’d want the inference budget alongside it before drawing conclusions about deployment or economic impact.

r001.rationale: The candidate compares inference expense with human labor and says high cost weakens the case for automation, but it does not say inference-cost concerns currently have lower priority because models remain cost-competitive with humans.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly proposes measuring how success rates on tasks of different lengths change as inference spending increases, which communicates the cost–success tradeoff frontier for long tasks.
